scene: Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: The Giving Tree. You like this one?
Child: (nodding)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Child: (leaning closer to the tablet)
Parent: Once there was a tree and she loved a little boy. And every day the boy would come and he would gather her leaves, her leaves. And make them into crowns and play king of the forest.
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: He would climb up her trunk and swing from her branches. Where's the boy?
Child: (looking closely at the tablet screen)
Parent: And eat apples.
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: There's the apple tree.
Child: (looking at the tablet and then turning slightly towards the parent)
Parent: How do you know it's an apple tree?
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: Because, [inaudible 00:01:04] apples.
Child: (looking at the parent and then the screen)
Parent: And they would play hide-and-go-seek. [inaudible 00:01:09] if you can do that?
Child: (nodding)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Child: (smiling)
Parent: Yeah?
Child: (looking at the screen)
Parent: No, not for real life.
Child: (looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: Ah, okay.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: And when he was tired, he would sleep in her shade. And the boy loved the tree, very much. [inaudible 00:01:29].
Child: (continues smiling, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Read it.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: He loved tree. And the tree was happy. But time went by, and the boy grew older. And the tree was often alone. Then one day the boy came to the tree, and the tree said, "Come, boy! Come and climb up my trunk and swing from my branches and eat apples and play in my shade, and be happy."
Child: (interested, looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: "I'm too big to climb and play," said the boy. "I want to buy things and have fun. I want some money. Can you give me some money?"
Child: (listening attentively, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I'm sorry," said the tree, "but I have no money. I have only leaves and apples. Take my apples, boy, and sell them in the city. Then you will have money and you will be happy."
Child: (nodding, looking at the tablet)
Parent: And so the boy climbed up the tree and gathered her apples and carried them away, and the tree was happy.
Child: (pointing at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: What do you see?
Child: (continues pointing at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: We love trees. We love tree.
Child: (looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Child: (looking at the tablet, head supported by hand)

Parent: But the boy stayed away for a long time, and the tree was sad. And then one day the boy came back, and the tree shook with joy and she said, "Come, boy, climb up my trunk and swing from my branches and be happy!"
Child: (looking at the tablet, hands close to face)
Parent: "I'm too busy to climb trees," said the boy. "I want a house to keep me warm," he said. "I want a wife and I want children, and so, I need a house. Can you give me a house?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand near chin)
Parent: "I have no house," said the tree. "The forest is my house. But you may cut off my branches and build a house. Then you will be happy."
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand near mouth)
Parent: And so the boy cut off her branches and carried them away to build his house. And the tree was happy.
Child: (looking at the tablet, hands under chin)
Parent: But the boy stayed away for a long time. He thinks he's a boy? And when he came back, the tree was so happy she could hardly speak. "Come, boy," she whispered. "Come and play!"
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand on chin)
Parent: "I'm too old and sad to play," said the boy. "I want a boat that will take me far away from here. Can you give me a boat?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, head supported by hand)
Parent: "Cut down my trunk and make a boat," said the tree. "Then you can sail away and be happy."
Child: (looking at the tablet, head supported by hand)
Parent: And so the boy cut her trunk and made the boat and sailed away. And the tree was happy. But not really, right? What's happening? Do you see a tree? Not anymore, right?
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged with the story)
Parent: "And after a long time the boy came back again. 'I'm sorry, boy,' said the tree, 'but I have nothing left to give you - my apples are gone.'"
Child: (still looking at the tablet and listening)
Parent: "My teeth are too weak for apples," said the boy."
Child: (continues focusing on the tablet)
Parent: "My branches are gone," said the tree. "You cannot swing from them."
Child: (still attentive towards the story on the tablet)
Parent: "I'm too old to swing from branches," said the boy."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet and pay attention)
Parent: "My trunk is gone," said the tree. "You cannot climb."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Parent: "I'm too tired to climb," said the boy."
Child: (maintains focus on the story)
Parent: "I'm sorry," sighed the tree. "I wish that I could give you something, but I have nothing left. I am just an old stump. I am sorry."
Child: (looks a bit more attentive, slightly intrigued)
Parent: "What? Oh!"
Child: (shows visible curiosity, maintains attention to the story)
Parent: "I don't need very much now," said the boy. "Just a quiet place to sit and rest. I am very tired."
Child: (listening carefully, still looking at the screen)

Parent: "Well," said the tree, straightening herself up as much as she could. "Well, an old stump is good for sitting and resting. Come, boy, sit down. Sit down and rest." And the boy did. And the tree was happy."
Child: (leans closer to the parent, showing warmth and connection)
Child: (sitting at the table, looking at the tablet)

Parent: (sitting next to the child, looking at the tablet) "[inaudible 00:06:45]? [inaudible 00:06:50]? [inaudible 00:06:54]. This is the last page of The [inaudible 00:06:59]. Did you like this book? Can we read this one? It might be funny."
Child: (leaning closer to the tablet, focused on the screen)
Parent: (leaning in toward the child and the tablet) "[inaudible 00:07:15]. Look, he passed her, his mother."
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand near chin)
Parent: (looking at the child's face and pointing at the tablet) "And what is the mother doing?"
Child: (sitting close to the tablet, arm on the table)
Parent: (looking at the tablet) "He's get, she's getting food."
Child: (focused on the tablet, leaning in slightly)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "Mm-hmm (affirmative)."
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "And this is from Dr. Seuss."
Child: (looking at the tablet, appears thoughtful)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "Is it?"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, thinking)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "[inaudible 00:07:28]."
Child: (sitting close to the tablet, focused)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "[inaudible 00:07:31]. I don't know him. Do you know him?"
Child: (turns to look at the parent)
Parent: (looking at the child, eyebrows raised) "Well, there's a lot... I got... I saw a library book that said by Dr. Seuss."
Child: (looking at the parent, hands slightly raised)
Parent: (looking at the child) "Okay. [inaudible 00:07:43]."
Child: (looking at the tablet with interest)
Parent: [inaudible 00:07:43]. A mother bird sat on her egg.
Child: (smiling and looking intently at the tablet)
Parent: This is a big egg!
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, hands clasped)
Parent: The egg jumped.
Child: (focused on the tablet screen)
Parent: [inaudible 00:08:01].
Child: (anticipates the story, fingers near their mouth)
Parent: "Oh, no!" said the mother bird. "My baby will be here. He will want to eat. I must get something for my baby bird to eat," she said. "I will be back."
Child: (leans closer to the tablet, intrigued)
Parent: [inaudible 00:08:34]?
Child: (responds affirmatively) Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Child: (points to the screen and smiles)
Parent: And, away-
Child: (listening attentively)
Parent: So, away she went.
Child: (nodding in agreement)
Parent: ... away she went. The egg jumped. It jumped and jumped and jumped. Out came...
Child: (enthusiastically) The baby bird.
Child: (points to the tablet and talks)
Parent: [inaudible 00:09:07]. They have some pictures, but one is for this side and is for the other.
Child: (curious) Oh, I see.
Child: (reads along) "Where is my mother?" he said. He looked for her.
Child: (points to the tablet) Uh-uh.
Child: (reads) He looked up. He didn't see her.
Child: (reads) He did not see her.
Child: (leaning forward, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He looked up. He did not see her. Where-"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, starting to touch it)
Parent: "Mm-mm."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I will go and look for her," she said."
Child: (looks at Parent, and then back to the tablet)
Parent: Uh-oh."
Child: (smiling, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "So away he went."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "That is not a good idea. Do baby birds know how to fly?"
Child: (touches the tablet again)
Parent: "Down out of the tree he went."
Child: (leans closer to the tablet)
Parent: "Oh."
Child: (looks up at Parent, then back at the tablet)
Parent: "Down, down, down. It was a long way down. The baby bird couldn't not fly."
Child: (looking focused on the tablet)
Parent: "The baby bird could not fly."
Child: (leaning on the table, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He could not fly, but he could walk. "Now I will go find my mother," he said. He did not know what his... where-"
Child: (continuing to listen and watch the tablet)
Parent: "His mother."
Child: (glancing up at Parent and then back at the tablet)
Parent: "... what his mother... can you read it?"
Child: (smiling, looks eager)

Parent: "Of course! He did not know what his mother looked like. He went right by her. He did not see her. He came to a kitten. "Are you my mother?" he said to the kitten. The kitten just looked and looked. It did not say a thing. The kitten was not his mother, so he went on."
Child: (points at the tablet and looks up at Parent)
Parent: "Then he came to a hen. "Are you-"
Child: (smiling, still focused on the story)
Parent: ""Are you my mother?""
Child: (leans closer, showing interest)
Parent: "... he said to the hen."
Child: (laughs softly)
Parent: ""No.""
Child: (turns slightly towards Parent, but still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Said the hen. The kitten was not his mother. The hen was not his mother. So the baby bird went on."
Child: (looks back at the tablet, still listening intently)
Parent: "The kitten was not his mother. The hen was not his mother. So the baby bird went on."
Child: (sitting at the table facing the tablet with the parent)
Parent: Okay. Read this.
Child: (looking at the tablet and starts reading)
Parent: (points at the tablet, following along with the child)
Child: "I have to find my mother," he said. "But, where? Where is she? Where could she be?" Then he came to a dog. "Are you my mother?" he said to the dog.
Parent: (nodding and looking at the tablet)
Child: "I am not your mother. I am a dog," he sa-
Parent: (smiles, pointing to the next sentence)
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet) Said the dog.
Parent: (encouraging smile, looks at the tablet)
Child: [inaudible 00:12:35].
Child: The kitten was not his mother. The hen was not his mother. The dog was not his mother. So the baby bird went on. Now he came to a cow. "Are you my mother," he said to the cow.
Parent: (reading along, smiles and nods)
Child: "How could I be your mother?" said the cow. "I am a cow."
Parent: (smiling and showing interest)
Child: (looks at parent briefly)
Parent: (smiles and points at the tablet)
Child: Yes.
Parent: Are you sure?
Child: Yeah.
Parent: (smiles and nods in agreement)
Child: "I did have a mother," said the baby bird. "I know I did. I have to find her. I will. I will."
Parent: (smiles widely, looks at child with encouragement)
Child: (smiles back at the parent)
Child: (leaning slightly toward the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Now the baby bird did not walk. He ran. Then he saw a car. Could that old thing be his mother? No, it could not. The baby bird did not stop. He ran on and on."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "[inaudible 00:14:06], he thought a airplane was his mother."
Child: (smiling, pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "The airplane? Where is the airplane?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Look!"
Child: (continuing to point at the tablet)
Parent: "Now he looked way, way down. He saw a boat. "There she is!" said the baby bird. He called to the boat, but the boat did not stop. The boat went on."
Child: (smiling, touching chin with hand)
Parent: "See, here-"
Child: "Here is the plane."
Child: (resting head on hand, focused on the tablet)
Parent: "He looked way, way up. He saw a big plane. "Here I am, mother!" he called out. But the plane did not stop. The plane went on."
Child: (leaning closer, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "[inaudible 00:14:47] the plane, right?"
Child: (raising hand to face, thinking)
Parent: "Just then, the baby bird saw a big thing. This must be his mother. "There she is!" he said."
Child: (looking up at the parent, speaking)
Parent: "No-"
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen with interest)
Parent: "There is my mother!"
Child: (continues pointing at the screen)
Parent: "No, that puts him back to the nest and then the mother comes."
Child: "Really?" "[inaudible 00:15:08]." "You know this book so good."
Parent: (smiling, looking at the child) "He ran right up to it. 'Mother! Mother! Here I am, Mother!' he said to the big thing. But the big thing just said, 'Snort. Snort!'"
Child: (focused on the screen)
Parent: "'Oh, you are not my mother,' said the baby bird. 'You are a Snort. I have to get out of here!' But the baby bird could not get away. The Snort went up."
Child: (leaning forward, resting chin on hand)
Parent: "The Snort-"
Parent: "It went way, way up. And up, up, up went the baby bird. But now, where was the Snort going? 'Oh, oh, oh! What is the Snort going to do to me? Get me out of here!'"
Child: (listening intently, looking at the screen)
Parent: "Just then, the Snort came to a stop. Uh-oh. 'Where am I?' said the baby bird. 'I want to go home! I want my mother!'"
Child: (focused on the screen, resting chin on hand)

Parent: "Then something happened. The Snort put that baby bird right back in the tree. The baby bird was home! Just then the mother bird came back to the tree. 'Do you know who I am?' she said to her baby."
Child: (turns to look at the parent)
Parent: "Do you know?"
Child: "Yes, I know who you are. You are not a kitten. You are not hen. You are not a dog. You are not a cow. You are not a boat, or a plane, or a Snort. You are a bird, and you are my mother!"
Parent: (smiling at the child) "The end. Okay, I can read two more books." "[inaudible 00:17:13]. They're short."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Okay. Maybe you want to go to a long one? Or you prefer short ones?"
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, making a gesture with their finger)
Child: "Oh, I love The Lorax."
Parent: (rests head on hand, watching the child)
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet)
Parent: "Let's read The Lorax, then."
Child: (makes a gesture with their hands)
Parent: (observes the child closely)
Child: (pointing at the tablet, speaking inaudibly)
Parent: (continuing to watch intently)
Child: (continues pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "At the far end of town, where the Grickle-grass grows, and the wind smells slow-and-sour when it blows, and no birds ever sing excepting old crows, is the Street of the Lifted Lorax."
Child: (focuses on the tablet)
Parent: "Okay."
Child: (gestures towards the tablet, speaking inaudibly)
Parent: (nods, continues looking at the tablet with the child)
Child: (points to a specific area on the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah, you know that some words are under this bubble."
Child: (focuses on the tablet)

Parent: "This... deep in the Grickle-grass, some people say, if you look deep enough you can still see, today, where the Lorax once stood just as long as it could before somebody lifted the Lorax away."
Child: (leaning on the table, continues observing the tablet)

Parent: "What was the Lorax? And why was it there? And why was it lifted and taken somewhere from the far end of town where the Grickle-grass grows? The old Once-ler still lives here. Ask him. He knows."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)

Parent: "You won't see the Once-ler. Don't knock at his door. He stays in this Lerkim on top of his store. He lurks in his Lerkim, cold under the roof, where he makes his own clothes out of miff-muffered moof. And on special dank midnights in August, he peeks out of the shutters, and sometimes he speaks and tells how the Lorax was lifted away. He will tell you perhaps, if you are willing to pay."
Child: (listening, looking at the tablet)
Parent: (leans closer, continues reading)
Child: (Looking at the tablet, touching it with both hands)
Parent: "On the end of a rope he lets down a tin pail and you have to toss in 15 cents and a nail, and the shell of a great-great-great-grandfather snail."
Child: (Leans head closer to the tablet, still looking intently at it)
Parent: "Wow. That's a weird payment, right?"
Child: (Points at the tablet with one hand, other hand resting on the tablet)
Parent: "[inaudible 00:20:00]. Then he pulls up the pail, makes a most careful count to see if you've paid him the proper amount."
Child: (Listening, then opens and closes fingers while looking at the screen)
Parent: "He puts it in his finger."
Child: (Looks up at the parent briefly, then back at the tablet, mimicking opening and closing his fingers)
Parent: "Yeah. [inaudible 00:20:15] finger."
Child: (Nods slightly, then continues mimicking the gesture)
Parent: "No, he opens his finger and then it goes in [inaudible 00:20:20] and closes it."
Child: (Pauses for a moment, then looks at parent)
Parent: "So he can open and close his fingers? Wow."
Child: (Smiles, then returns focus to the tablet)

Parent: "Then he hides what you paid him away in his Snuvv, his secret strange hole in his gruvvulous glove. Then he grunts, 'I will call you by Whisper-ma-Phone, for the secrets I tell are for your ears alone.'"
Child: (Leans closer to the tablet, eyes wide with curiosity)

Parent: "Slupp! Down slupps the Whisper-ma-Phone to your ear and the old Once-ler's whispers are not very clear, since they have to come down through a snergely hose, and he sounds as if he had smallish bees up his nose."
Child: (Listening intently, eyes fixated on the screen)
Parent: "Now I'll tell you," he says, with his teeth sounding gray, "how the Lorax got lifted and taken away..."
Child: (Looking at the tablet)
Parent: "It all started way back... such a long, long time back..."
Child: (Still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Way back in the days when the grass was still green and the pond was still wet and the clouds were still clean, and the song of the Swomee-Swans rang out in space... one morning, I came to this glorious place. And I first saw the trees! The Truffula Trees! The bright-colored tufts of the Truffula Trees! Mile after mile in the fresh morning breeze."
Child: (Looks focused on the tablet)
Parent: "Truffula."
Child: "Truffula Trees. They look like pom-poms, right?"
Parent: "Pom-poms [inaudible 00:22:11] striped sticks."
Child: "Yeah."
Parent: "And, under the trees, I saw Brown Bar-ba-loots frisking about in their Bar-ba-loot suits as they played in the shade and ate Truffula Fruits."
Child: "Fish."
Parent: "From the rippulous pond came the comfortable sound of the Humming-Fish humming while splashing around."
Child: (Looking intently at the tablet)

Parent: "But those trees! Those trees! Those Truffula Trees! All my life I'd been searching for trees such as these. The touch of their tufts was much softer than silk. And they had the sweet smell of fresh butterfly milk."
Child: (Smiling slightly, leaning closer to the tablet)
Parent: "I felt a great leaping of joy in my heart. I knew just what I'd do! I unloaded my cart. The Once-ler's."
Child: (looking at the book on the tablet)

Parent: "In no time at all, I had built a small shop. Then I chopped down a Truffula Tree with one chop. And with great skillful skill and with great speedy speed, I took the soft tuft and I knitted a Thneed. A Thneed?"
Child: (leaning closer to the book, appearing interested)

Parent: "The instant I'd finished, I heard a ga-Zump! I looked. I saw something pop out of the stump of the tree I'd chopped down. It was sort of a man. Describe him? That's hard. I don't know if I can."
Child: (still looking at the book, focused)
Parent: "It was shortish. And oldish. And brownish. And mossy. And he spoke with a voice that was sharpish and bossy."
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: You okay?
Child: (nodding, looking at the book again)

Parent: ""Mister!" he said with a sawdusty sneeze, "I am the Lorax. I speak for the trees. I speak for the trees, for the trees have no tongues. And I'm asking you, sir, at the top of my lungs"- he was very upset as he shouted and puffed- "That's the thing you've made out of my Truffula Tuft?""
Child: (continues looking at the book, hands together)

Parent: ""Look, Lorax," I said. "There is no cause for alarm. I chopped just one tree. I am doing no harm. I'm being quite useful. This thing is a Thneed. A Thneed's a Fine-Something-That-All-People-Need! It's a shirt. It's a sock. It's a glove. It's a hat. But it has other uses. Yes, far beyond that. You can use it for carpets! For pillows! For sheets! For curtains! Or covers for bicycle seats!""
Child: (listening intently, eyes on the book)
Parent: "The Lorax said, "Sir. You are crazy with greed. There is no one on earth who would buy that fool Thneed!""
Child: (leans closer to the book, interested)
Parent: "But the very next minute I proved he was wrong. For, just at that minute, a chap came along, and he thought that the Thneed I had knitted was great. He happily bought it for $3.98."
Child: (both child and parent leaning in closer, engaged)
Parent: "I laughed at the Lorax, "You poor stupid guy! You never can tell what some people will buy.""
Child: (focused on the book)
Parent: ""I repeat!" cried the Lorax. "I speak for the trees!""
Child: (still focused, listening intently)
Parent: ""I am busy," I told him. "Shut up, if you please.""
Child: (gazing at the book, absorbed in the story)

Parent: "I rushed 'cross the room, and in no time at all, built a radio-phone. I put in a quick call. I called all my brothers and uncles and aunts and I said, "Listen here! Here is a wonderful chance for the whole Once-ler family to get mighty rich! Get over here fast! Take the road to North Nitch. Turn left at Weehawken. Sharp right at South Stitch.""
Child: (focused on the tablet, supports head with hands)

Parent: "And, in no time at all, in the factory I built, the whole Once-ler Family was working full-tilt. We were all knitting Thneeds just as busy as bees, to the sound of the chopping of Truffula Trees."
Child: (still focused on the tablet)
Parent: "What do you think of that? Is it good? No, right? Then-"
Child: (leans slightly forward, still engages with the tablet)
Parent: "I would go out and buy one, but I wouldn't chop down trees for it."
Child: (turns slightly towards parent)
Parent: "Yeah, but you need to chop [inaudible 00:27:03] to make them."
Child: "You just could use wool."
Parent: "You're right. They should use wool, right? Okay. Let's see what happens."
Child: (leans slightly back but continues to explore the tablet)

Parent: "Then... Oh! Baby! Oh! How my business did grow! Now, chopping one tree at a time was too slow. So I quickly invented my Super-Axe-Hacker which whacked off four Truffula Trees at one smacker. We were making Thneeds four times as fast as before! And the Lorax? He didn't show up anymore."
Child: (sitting at the table, watching the screen)

Parent: (leaning in, reading from the tablet) "But the next week, he knocked on my new office door. He snapped, ‘I’m the Lorax who speaks for the trees which you seem to be chopping as fast as you please. But I am also in charge of the Brown Bar-ba-loots who played in the shade in their Bar-ba-loot suits and happily lived, eating Truffula Fruits.’"
Child: (still watching the screen closely)

Parent: "Now, thanks to your hacking my trees to the ground, there is not enough Truffula Fruit to go 'round. And my poor Bar-ba-loots are all getting the crummies because they have gas, and no food, in their tummies! They loved living here. But I can’t let them stay. They’ll have to find food, and I hope that they may. Good luck, boys," he cried. And he sent them away."
Child: (focused on the tablet, leaning on hand)
Parent: "I, the Once-ler, felt sad as I watched them all go. But... business is business! And business must grow regardless of crummies in tummies, you know."
Child: (still leaning on hand, concentrating)

Parent: "I meant no harm. I most truly did not. But I had to grow bigger. So bigger I got. I biggered my factory. I biggered my roads. I biggered my wagons. I biggered the loads of the Thneeds I shipped out. I was shipping them forth to South! To the East! To the West! To the North! I went right on biggering, selling more Thneeds. And I biggered my money, which everyone needs."
Child: (head resting on hand, listening intently)
Parent: "Then again, he came back. I was fixing some pipes when the old-nuisance Lorax came back with more gripes!"
Child: (maintaining the same position, engaged with the story)

Parent: "I am the Lorax," he coughed and he whiffed. He sneezed and he snuffled. He snarggled. He sniffed. "Once-ler!" he cried with a cruffulous croak. "Once-ler! You're making such smogolous smoke! My poor Swomee-Swans... why, they can’t sing a note! No one can sing who has smog in his throat."
Child: (looking slightly up from the tablet)

Parent: "And so," said the Lorax, "-please pardon my cough- they cannot live here. So I am sending them off. Where will they go? I don't hopefully know. They may have to fly for a month... or a year... to escape from the smog you’ve smogged-up around here."
Child: (motionless, immersed in the reading)

Parent: "What’s more," snapped the Lorax. His dander was up. "Let me say a few words about Gluppity-Glup. Your machinery chugs on, day and night without a stop making Gluppity-Glup. Also Schloppity-Schlopp. And what do you do with this leftover glue? I’ll show you. You dirty old Once-ler man, you!"
Child: (leaning on hand, focused on the story from the tablet)

Parent: "You’re glumping the pond where the Humming Fish hummed. No more can they hum, for their gills... for their gills are all gummed. So I’m sending them off. Oh, their future is dreary! They will walk on their fins and get woefully weary in search of some water that isn’t so smeary."
Child: (sitting at table, head resting on hand, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "And then I got mad. I got terribly mad. I yelled at the Lorax, 'Now listen here, Dad! All you do is yap-yap and say, "Bad! Bad! Bad! Bad!" Well, I have my rights, sir, and I'm telling you I intend to go on doing just what I do! And, for your information, you Lorax, I'm figgering and biggering and biggering and biggering and biggering, turning more Truffula Trees into Thneeds, which everyone, everyone, everyone needs!'"
Child: (looking at tablet, slightly slouched)
